utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. As usual, I'm asking you whether you can hear me in a language that you can understand. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. I think we may have the case called now, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours, and I hope this is only a temporary accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, too. Good morning to you, Ms. Korner. I really feel cramped in this courtroom, but anyway it's one of the three that we have and sometimes we have to work here. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, representing General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. So before we go into closed session, there is one small matter that I wanted to raise with you. Particularly it will become a question to the Prosecution more than anything else. You will recall, Ms. Korner, that there is one motion pending, which we discussed very, very briefly here, and that is the motion filed by the Defence teams for Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic to have access to trial transcripts and so on and so forth. And the decision has been drafted. More or less, it's not a controversial matter at all. There is one point that has been brought up, and that relates as to the time frame for which our decision will be applicable. In other words, there is the tendency, based on past experience, that when this Trial Chamber will eventually grant the motion to Krajisnik and Plavsic, the access would be operative, would be effective, only with regard to those documents, transcripts, existing up to a certain time, with the result, and it seems that a very strict interpretation or reading of the relevant rule would entail -- would point in the -- indicate such a way of determining the issue. I was actually thinking -- I mean I discussed it briefly with the Senior Legal Officer, and we agreed to put it to you, to see whether you would -- it's not only a crammed room but you can barely move one inch backward because it will start pulling here -- whether it will be at all possible for us to say that, with regard to transcripts, with regard to the basic documents that will be forthcoming, the decision will be effective for the whole duration of the trial, reserving for the Prosecution the right, should there be one or more documents where you may have submissions to make or reservations to make, to bring -- or to bring that matter up as we go along and when these cases arise. That would spare us having to receive, practically on a monthly basis, similar -- identical motions to this one, which have to go to your office and you have to prepare also a reply and then it comes to us and we also have to draft another decision. If we could avoid all this, I think we can only avoid it if there is consensus amongst you, particularly forthcoming from your side, that there would be no objection from the Prosecution for the -- for the Chamber to make available these documents throughout the whole trial, excepting those which we may need to discuss as we go along. I don't necessarily want you to tell me yes or no now, obviously because this is a matter that I'm only raising now and I understand that you didn't come here prepared to give me a clear answer. But I would suggest to you to think about it and to come back to us. I think we -- I think reading the Rule, there is space for us to decide in such a fashion. But I wouldn't risk deciding so unless there is the -- the consensus of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just make sure I understand. And I'm grateful for Your Honour saying we could have some time to just consider it. As I recall our response, it was no objection save insofar as there were confidential exhibits and/or witnesses and that the onus should be on those requesting to show why they required them. As I understand it, Your Honour is suggesting it should be the other way round, that the Prosecution should make a showing as to why it shouldn't be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting the other way round. In fact, this is -- this is the -- what is brought about it and what we discussed, the senior legal officer and myself. We are definitely not shifting the burden, no. We do not intend to shift the burden. What we are trying to do is that there are some documents which out of their own nature would not require another motion or a monthly motion, such as the transcripts of the sittings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are also documents which in themselves are not confidential in any way. And again, I don't see why as they are brought forward and introduced in the records of this case as exhibits we have to every month decide on those -- on those. What I was suggesting was that as you bring in the records or as you introduce documents which you may have reservations about or which -- on which you are quite categoric that you don't want to have these included, you will indicate these to us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or to the Prosecution -- or to the Defence, so the Defence know that there is a problem with regard to these documents and with regard to these documents only. And in that case, we would have a motion relating to those documents only and not regarding the rest. That would avoid us having to receive I can't imagine how many motions, you know, because these confidential documents will be arriving every so often, but not as often as the transcripts or the documents which are not confidential. So what the Trial Chamber would be asking from you -- not exactly shifting the -- just indicating, indicating that -- to the Defence that there is no consensus on the Prosecution for the disclosure of these documents to Krajisnik and -- yes, then we'll decide -- we'll decide that issue as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I say that with respect to the exhibits, the ordinary exhibits, I have little doubt that the Krajisnik/Plavsic team have them anyhow, because I know that disclosure by the Prosecution team in that case has been following ours to a large extent, although it covers a wider area. Your Honour, my only concerns are that it -- there are some witnesses and some documents which will reveal their identity about which we have more concern than others, those who Judge Hunt granted us late disclosure because of their sensitivity. Your Honour, I think if Your Honour would be kind enough, I can certain give you an answer by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And feel free to say "No, definitely not." We wouldn't be surprised in the least. In other words, we are prepared for it. The decision is ready either way; in other words, either one way or another. We feel more comfortable in deciding also for the future if there is the hundred per cent consensus on your part. If there isn't, we wouldn't like to establish a precedent in this field. Rather than explore fresh ground, we would rather stick to what the practice has been.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we're mindful of the fact, as you rightly say, that written motions are bad enough for those that are really necessary. And if we can dispense with some that may not be necessary, we should. And we'll certainly make inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks, Ms. Korner. So I think we could bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The motion you requested on Friday has been prepared and will be filed today regarding the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you. I think we need to go into closed session now even before the witness arrives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- just before he comes in, we did file on Friday the response to Mr. Ackerman's motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 90(H).

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope it will be given to Your Honours today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's quite a long one-page response, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We thought we'd preempt the appeal brief slightly. But if Your Honours would be minded perhaps to give that consideration as one of the first so that we'll all know where we stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we go in open session for a short while, please

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, Madam Fauveau, I found on my desk the Prosecution's ninth motion for protective measures in relation to witness disclosure number 7.118. Are you familiar with this motion as yet or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I read it very briefly this morning, Your Honour, so yes, I am -- I would say that I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same for me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am suggesting the same manner of proceeding that I did -- like I did about a week or two ago. If you -- there are no objections on your part, could we go ahead and -- if there are, just tell me, and it will take its normal course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I was reading it this morning, I was perhaps reading it more carefully than I have recent ones. It's my recollection -- and I intended to go back this afternoon and look -- it was my recollection that Judge Hunt had taken the position that it was an insufficient basis for these kind of measures if it was purely the witness's statement that he might be in danger for one reason or another, that there had to be something objective beyond the mere statement of a witness. I believe that's what Judge Hunt said. And looking at this request, I think it is in that category, that the witness is just saying he thinks it would be a situation that might put him in some danger. So I think it has to go beyond that. I have taken the position in the pre-trial portions of this case, and in many ways Judge Hunt has agreed, that these proceedings should be public as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, there I agree too, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that it should be extraordinary when we make them not public, and that just the mere assertion by a witness - I think Judge Hunt said - is not sufficient. But I wouldn't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- tell you that without looking it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But I would refer you to para 2 of -- para numbered 2 in the submissions in this ninth Prosecution motion, which goes beyond what you have just mentioned. In other words, it specifies at least one -- two particular reasons why the protective measure was requested by the witness and now by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I point out, this witness is not a live witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- under Rule 92. I'm not even sure that we've decided on the exact procedure how they're going to be dealt with. Judge Hunt's order dealt with the disclosure to the Defence of witness identities. Your Honour, all we can say, as we've said in that motion, is that witness has expressed concerns. It might be a different matter if the witness were to testify live. It may be that Your Honour felt that those concerns were not enough. Our simple application is on the basis that he has concerns, real concerns. His statement is -- I don't know if it's going to be read into the record or how it's going to be. I'm not sure. But all I was concerned was whether it was necessary from an open justice point of view to have this witness's identity disclosed to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I'll leave you time to think about it. If you think at the end of the day or whenever we can proceed along the same lines as last time, we will do that. Obviously if not, you will have the usual time to reply and make submissions, and then we will decide it later on in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suspect that that's where I'm going to be. I'd like to have until morning to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I think Ms. Korner is correct. I think there probably is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- with regard to a 92 bis situation rather than with a live witness. Not having thought it through, just give me till morning, and I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The same applies to you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not oppose this request of the Prosecutor. But in future, we would like to have it, if it is possible, to have the testimony in an open session, whether it is Rule 92 bis or whether this is a testimony here by the witness. But we very much appreciate open sessions. But at the moment, we are not opposing this motion of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. So I think we can go in closed session now and bring in the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Archbold is still around, isn't it? We still have it. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I took the opportunity to get the copy of our motion and to discuss the matter with Mr. Cayley, in particular. Your Honour, there are effectively two sorts of witnesses who are going to be affected by this. One is those who will be testifying in open session but with various protective measures; and those that will be testifying, as today's witness, and the following two, in totally closed session. Your Honour, we don't want to be unhelpful about it, and in a sense we may not be, because most of the crime base witnesses who have pseudonyms or other types of protective measures are, in fact, the witnesses who will be used for Krajisnik and Plavsic. So we had a quick look at the two witness lists, and we think there are very few that the Defence team wouldn't get the identities of in any event, not mention the transcripts from here, because that would have to be disclosed as part of the testimony. In relation to the closed session witnesses, we have a feeling that much the same applies, that most of those have also been selected for the Krajisnik/Plavsic trial. We would ask at this stage, if Your Honours minded to say, that they must make a showing, to leave it at that. If it turns out that there are a lot where they're not getting the information or won't get it in the near future, well, then we would reconsider our position. But for the moment, Your Honour, the reason we have asked for these protective measures and Your Honours have been granting them is because there's a good reason why one doesn't want this to get into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That, I actually understand. I mean, and to tell you the truth -- I mean, I put it to you this morning for a very simple reason. I told you we have the two drafts ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I won't tell you what our preference is, obviously, because that's another issue. I do realise that there may be problems. I also do realise that possibly there is a bulk of documents, particularly transcripts, not of closed sessions -- I mean, because again, I see problems there. But I do realise that there may be problems. But I think at the -- at this point, we would rather play it safe and leave things as they were. And as we go along now -- later on, if there is the need -- as there will be the need -- we will --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it turns out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- definitely -- okay. Ms. Korner. I mean, the intention was certainly not to put the Prosecution at a disadvantage or to create problems for the Prosecution. That was definitely not the intention. The intention was to try and see if there could be a way of streamlining. However, if the situation remains that even as far as certain documents are concerned, there's still going to be the need for the Defence of those two individuals to file a motion -- it's not worth its while going through all this exercise now. And we will take it as we go along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, in fact, they filed their motion without appreciating that they would in any event get most of these transcripts through disclosure in their case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I don't know enough about their case to be able to appreciate. But I did then, while we were elaborating the judgement, realise that there is a quite substantial chunk of the evidence which is common to both, and we thought there might be this kind of -- but it's not a problem to us. We can live with it without any problems at all. And we will take it up as we go along. As there's the other subsequent motions, we'll start --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, we will certainly reconsider our position as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I think we can call it a day. Tomorrow morning you will commence with your cross-examination. Do you figure you will finish it tomorrow, conclude your examination -- cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it will take two or three hours, but it will obviously depend on the answers of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we should -- we should be able to make it. In any case, I think you ought to -- yes, we ought to think of whether -- because if it's three hours, you have the first two sessions, basically: 9.00 to 10.30, and then 11.00 to 12.30. So that is three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would hope, and I think -- you know, I appreciate that Madam Fauveau is giving an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: An indication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- an indication. But I would hope that it wouldn't take quite that long. I have some re-examination but not a lot. But in any event, I'm going to arrange for the next witness to be brought here by, I would say, the end of the first break, so from around 11.00 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So that is it. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. I thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 1.37 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
